boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Cumberland Church record (April 7, 1865) in the Appomattox Campaign [March-April 1865]. Humphreys, the historian, is the frozen Union commander of this record and narrates his own orders; his account is a self-interested participant's. High Bridge (VA095) is the same morning. Army-wide returns, campaign-wide loss and prisoner totals, the April 9 paroles and the retreat as a whole are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads 'Corps' and the live field zero. Humphreys says he came up with Miles's and De Trobriand's divisions, with Barlow detached toward Farmville, and informed Meade that Lee's whole remaining force, probably about 18,000 infantry, was before him, with Mahone's division on the left, Poague's sixteen guns and Gordon's and Longstreet's troops; Miles names the three regiments of his First Brigade that charged.
claims.rationale: Humphreys' 18,000 is his contemporary estimate of Lee's army-wide infantry, not a count at Cumberland Church. None is adopted as a matched opening strength; live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Confederate victory. Miles says the charge failed and a Confederate pursuit over the works was driven back; Humphreys says the Second Corps detained Lee from midday to night and that Lee moved off in the night, and that Crook's cavalry was attacked north of the river and Gregg captured.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. Humphreys' claim that the detention cost Lee time is a campaign-contribution judgment, not the tactical result.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 910 (US 655; CS 255) and the live field 571 (US 571; CS 0). Humphreys gives the Second Corps' loss for the whole day as 571 killed, wounded and missing, which matches the live Union figure but includes High Bridge and Barlow's fight near Farmville, where Smyth was mortally wounded; he names Brigadier-General Lewis among the Confederate wounded prisoners. Miles lists one gun captured on the march that day.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Humphreys' day total spans VA095 and VA094 and is not assigned to either alone.

open_questions: Humphreys' own report (No. 21), Barlow's and De Trobriand's reports (Nos. 54, 67), Crook's and Gregg's reports (Nos. 208, 211), Mahone's, Poague's and Fitzhugh Lee's accounts of April 7 (Fitzhugh Lee's selected; cited under other records), the Grant-Lee letters of April 7 and the returns remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC (the live NPS page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Humphreys' The Virginia Campaign of ’64 and ’65 (1883) is an interested history by the commander of the Second Corps in this campaign, in the same author family as the registered From Gettysburg to the Rapidan; where it narrates his own corps it is a participant's account. It relies on the reports of Sheridan, Warren, Wright, Gibbon, Ewell and Fitzhugh Lee, on Confederate testimony before the Warren Court of Inquiry and on the returns, so it is not independent of those families. Lee's, Sheridan's, Bushrod Johnson's, Miles's, Gibbon's, Ewell's and Fitzhugh Lee's papers, printed in Official Records Series I, Volume XLVI, Part 1, are separate families of interested commanders' accounts; the volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
